subject: mathematics
question_text: If f(x) = 1/x and g(x) = √x for all x ∈ (0, ∞), find (gof)(x).

Only the question was taken. recall_prompt: Say how you would find (gof)(x) here — which function acts first, and why the domain (0, ∞) matters.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Work f first and check the sign
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two things earn it: f(x) = 1/x as the inner value, and the sentence that 1/x is positive on (0, ∞) so the square root exists.
steps.memory_tip: In gof, f is inside. Here f makes 1/x, and the domain (0, ∞) keeps 1/x positive.
lines: For x ∈ (0, ∞) we have x > 0, so 1/x > 0.
A positive number has a real square root,

recall.must_convey: That f is the inner function giving 1/x, and that on (0, ∞) this value is positive, so the square root is a real number.

steps.why: The domain (0, ∞) is what makes this composition a real valued function. If x were 0 then 1/x would not exist, and if x were negative then 1/x would be negative and its square root would not be a real number.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the two functions and writing (√x)(1/x) instead of composing them.
Allowing x = 0, where 1/x is not defined.

steps.label: Apply g to 1/x
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Either √(1/x) or 1/√x is a correct final form; the simplified 1/√x is the one to box, with the domain written beside it.
steps.memory_tip: √(a/b) = √a/√b for positive a and b, and √1 = 1, so √(1/x) = 1/√x.

recall.must_convey: That g takes the square root of 1/x, which simplifies to 1 over root x.

steps.why: The square root of a quotient of positive numbers is the quotient of the square roots, and √1 = 1. Both √(1/x) and 1/√x name the same number for every x > 0.
common_mistakes: Leaving the domain x ∈ (0, ∞) off the final line.
